name: Femi Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Femi. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on response on the north-east side, which takes in the business park, the road out to the airport, and the stadium on match days. A shift could be a break-in at a warehouse, a crash on the airport road, then crowd duty with forty thousand people singing. I also trained last year as a drone pilot for the force, so a couple of times a month I fly the drone to search for a missing person or follow a stolen car. I love that part. What wears me out is the stop-start nature of it, sitting in a van for six hours then sprinting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a flat near my church, and at weekends I run personal training sessions at the community gym, six or seven clients, which brings in a bit extra. I use AI every day: it writes my clients' training plans, helps me revise for the sergeant's exam and runs my little investment app. My girlfriend Ruth works as an assistant at an accountancy firm. I've got about five months of money saved, and a small amount in shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. Huh. I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a good tool, like a good pair of boots, and you still have to walk. At work I'd tell people to use it for the boring bits and get on with policing. I post on my training page now and then, so I'd probably put up something about using it for fitness plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I carry on, and that's fine by me. The job's steady, the pay's fair, and the personal training brings in about three hundred a month. I'd like a bit more AI help than this picture gives, but my plans don't depend on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and keep flying the drone when they call me. I'd aim to grow the personal training to ten clients by next summer. And I'd keep putting a hundred a month into shares, because I like owning a slice of something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Picturing it, I'm at the gym on a Saturday morning with a client doing deadlifts, and life's going the way I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you like owning a slice of something. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents ran a small grocery shop when I was a kid, and my dad always said, work for a wage but own something too. He didn't trust anything he didn't own. I don't own a shop, but a few shares and a side business are my version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth make of this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would be relieved, because her work is all checking numbers. I'd tell my girlfriend Ruth she's safe for now, but to learn the tools anyway. She's careful with change, more careful than me.

say: AI is a **good tool**, like boots: you still have to walk.
Use it for the **boring bits** and get on with policing.
think: He can **carry on**, with a steady job and fair pay.
Personal training adds about **three hundred** a month.
do: Grow personal training to **ten clients** by next summer.
Keep investing **a hundred a month** in shares.
feel: **Calm**, life going the way he planned.
A bit **disappointed** there's less AI help than hoped.
S0.quote: AI is a good tool, like a good pair of boots, and you still have to walk.
fieldNote: Inherits his father's **ownership instinct**: wage plus a stake.
Already uses AI **daily** across work, study and his side business.
Secure job and a **side income** make him genuinely calm.

steps.text: Keep flying force drone searches on top of response shifts
Grow weekend personal training to ten clients by next summer
Put a hundred a month into shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Strong change but not a revolution. Okay. I can work with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the officers who learn the tools will do well and the ones who don't will struggle, and that's just how work goes. I'd say it kindly, and I'd offer to help anyone. I wouldn't call for government to protect jobs, I'd call for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. Drones and AI search tools would grow, and I'm already trained, so I'd push to move into the drone unit full-time. Ruth's job is the one I'd worry about, because accountancy assistants are exactly the thinking work this picture describes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the drone unit's next full-time post, and do the advanced flying course on my own time if needed. I'd use AI even more in the personal training, to handle bookings and messages, so I could take on more clients. And I'd help Ruth find a course in something AI won't take soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. A bit excited. The only shadow is Ruth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you suggest Ruth do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe move to the side of accounting where you talk to clients, small business owners who need someone they trust. Or something with her hands, she's always said she'd like to bake properly. I'd help pay for a course if she wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older officers who hate screens. I'd offer to sit with them, the way a corporal in my cadet days sat with me when I couldn't read a map. That's how you look after your own.

say: Officers who **learn the tools** will do well; that's how work goes.
think: The change is **good for him** as drones and AI search grow.
He'd aim for the **drone unit** full-time.
His girlfriend's **accountancy job** is directly exposed.
do: Apply for a **full-time drone post** and the advanced course.
Use AI for **bookings and messages** to take more clients.
Help Ruth find **a course** AI won't take soon.
S1.quote: The officers who learn the tools will do well and the ones who don't will struggle, and that's just how work goes.
fieldNote: Duty to colleagues framed as **looking after your own**.
Calm because his own drone and AI skills are **in demand** in this world.

steps.text: Apply for the next full-time post in the force drone unit
Use AI to handle personal training bookings and client messages
Take the advanced drone flying course in his own time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Two years. That's fast even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to prepare, not to panic or to beg for handouts. I'd tell people at work to learn whatever they can and to save. At church I'd say families should stick together through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, the drone unit gets automated quickly, because a flying camera with AGI doesn't need me holding the controls. The street work lasts till about 2031, then robots. I'm adaptable, but I can't adapt faster than the thing itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save harder, up to eight months, and stop putting money into shares for a while, because I want cash. I'd build the personal training into a proper business, fifteen clients, maybe a small group class, because people training people is hands-on and personal. And I'd propose to Ruth sooner rather than later, so we face it as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. I deal with worry by doing things, so I'd be doing a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the three years before robots. How do you plan around that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the window. Keep the police wage as the steady base, grow the training business on the side, and by 2031 have something that's mine. If robots can coach people by 2031 too, at least I'd own the gym membership list, which is worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why propose sooner, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to know who I'm facing it with. My parents got married in a hard year and always said it made them stronger. I'd tell my girlfriend Ruth it's not a panic decision, it's a priorities decision.

say: Now is the time to **prepare**, not panic or beg.
Families should **stick together**, he'd say at church.
think: AGI would **automate the drone unit** quickly.
Street work lasts till about **2031**, then robots.
He **can't adapt faster** than the change itself.
do: Save up to **eight months** and pause share buying.
Grow personal training to **fifteen clients** and a group class.
feel: **Anxious**, but handles it by staying busy.
S2.quote: I'm adaptable, but I can't adapt faster than the thing itself.
fieldNote: Sees his **drone skill** as more exposed than plain patrol.
Uses the **robot gap** as a window to build his own business.
Faith and **marriage** framed as strength, not just feeling.

steps.text: Pause share buying and save up to eight months in cash
Build personal training to fifteen clients and a group class
Propose to Ruth within the year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's still quick, but it's a runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for anyone willing to work at it. Learn, save, and don't wait for someone else to save you. I'd say it kindly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well enough. I'd get the sergeant's exam done by 2028, because the officers who manage the AI and the robots will be the last ones needed. The training business would keep growing on the side. Ruth has time to move into something more client-facing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit the sergeant's exam next year. I'd keep investing a hundred a month, and maybe buy a share in the community gym if the owner sells. And I'd keep using every AI tool going, so I understand what my team is using when I'm a supervisor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly focused. It's like a long training block before a race. You know the date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying into the gym is a big step. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people will still want to train with a person, at least till 2034, and the gym is the place where that happens. If I own a piece of the gym, I'm not just an employee of the change. My dad would call that good sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd be worried for in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Young lads on the estates near the stadium, the ones who'd have joined the police or the army in another time. If those jobs shrink, what do they do? Church and gyms can help, but they need a path.

say: Five years is enough for **anyone willing to work**.
Learn, save, and **don't wait** to be rescued.
He'd say it **kindly**, but he would say it.
think: Officers who **manage AI and robots** will be the last needed.
His training business keeps **growing on the side**.
Ruth has time to move into **client-facing** work.
do: Consider buying **a share** in the community gym.
Use every **AI tool** to supervise well later.
feel: Like **training for a race** with a known date.
S3.quote: If I own a piece of the gym, I'm not just an employee of the change.
fieldNote: Strategy is **ownership plus supervision**: sergeant and a gym stake.
Worries for **young men** whose usual paths might shrink.
Five years lets his adaptability **stay ahead** of events.

steps.text: Sit the sergeant's exam next year
Offer to buy a share of the community gym
Use every new force AI tool to prepare for supervising

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it can't blame the machines. I'd say prepare, own something, learn something. I'd say it at work and on my training page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's a good picture for me. By 2036 I'd hope to be a sergeant with a drone team, own part of a gym, and have a family. The robots around 2039 would change things again, but by then I'd have a base. Ruth and I would have time to plan properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep investing in shares and the business. I'd marry Ruth in a couple of years as planned and maybe buy a house around 2030. And I'd keep learning every tool as it comes, the way I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit excited. It feels like being given the exam questions early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're too relaxed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ten years can turn into six if things speed up. I'd check every year and switch to the five-year plan if I needed to. Being ready to change is my safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell young recruits joining in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young recruits to learn the tools, own something, and keep their faith and family close. The badge is a good job, but it shouldn't be your only plan.

say: Ten years is **a gift**; wasting it isn't the machines' fault.
He'd urge people to **own and learn** something.
think: By 2036 he'd hope to be **a sergeant** with a drone team.
He'd own **part of a gym** and have a family.
Robots in 2039 meet him with **a base** built.
do: Keep **investing** in shares and the business.
Marry Ruth and **buy a house** around 2030.
Keep learning **every tool** as it comes.
feel: Like being given **the exam questions** early.
S4.quote: The badge is a good job, but it shouldn't be your only plan.
fieldNote: Ten years fits his habit of **planning ahead**; the change looks good for him.
Admits he might be **too relaxed**, then names yearly checks.

steps.text: Keep buying shares and investing in the training business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my best skill, the drone, goes first and I'd have three years to build something else. What would help is fast, practical training, low-interest loans for people starting small businesses, and the force being honest early about which posts it's keeping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people own. Everyone asks about jobs, but if machines do the work, the people who own a slice of something are the ones who'll be all right. I'd want ordinary officers to own a bit too, not just the tech firms.

headlineQuote: If machines do the work, the people who own a slice of something are the ones who'll be all right.
portrait: A **27-year-old response officer** on the north-east side who also flies the force's **drone**.
Runs weekend **personal training**, invests a little and uses AI every day.
Traditional and churchgoing; prefers **training and ownership** to government protection.
Calm when change is slow; **anxious** when fast AGI automates his drone skill first.
Plans to propose to Ruth, whose **accountancy job** worries him more than his own.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which takes his drone skill first and leaves three years to rebuild.
whatWouldHelp: Early honesty from the force about **kept posts**.
